name: Optimising Yield and Rate
what: This subtopic addresses how to use Le Chatelier's principle to determine the conditions that maximise the yield of a desired product, and identifies the conflicts that can arise between optimising reaction rate and maximising equilibrium yield.
why: Optimising industrial reactions requires balancing competing factors. This topic directly connects VCE Chemistry theory to real-world industrial processes such as the Haber process and is a common focus of extended response questions.

items.title: I can determine the factors that maximise yield in a given equilibrium system using Le Chatelier's principle
items.what: Yield can be maximised by applying conditions that shift equilibrium toward the product side: using excess reactant, removing product as it forms, adjusting temperature in the direction favourable to the forward reaction, and adjusting pressure in favour of the side with fewer gas moles (if applicable).
items.why: Understanding how to maximise yield is a core industrial chemistry concept and is regularly assessed in VCE. It requires applying Le Chatelier's principle systematically across multiple variables at once.
items.example: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) = 2NH3(g) with delta H = -92 kJ mol^-1, yield is maximised by: using low temperature (favours exothermic forward reaction), high pressure (fewer gas moles on product side), excess N2 or H2, and continuous removal of NH3 as it forms.

items.title: I can identify potential conflicts between reaction rate and yield in a given equilibrium system
items.what: Conditions that improve rate may harm yield and vice versa. For example, high temperature increases reaction rate but decreases yield for an exothermic reaction. A compromise must be found between sufficient rate and acceptable yield.
items.why: In industrial chemistry, both rate and yield have economic significance. Recognising and articulating conflicts between them is directly required in VCE extended response questions, especially in the context of the Haber process.
items.example: For the Haber process, N2(g) + 3H2(g) = 2NH3(g): increasing temperature speeds up the reaction (improves rate) but shifts equilibrium to the left (decreases yield of NH3). The industrial compromise is a moderate temperature of approximately 400-500 degrees C, which balances both factors.

items.title: I can use graphical and thermochemical information together to determine optimal reaction conditions
items.what: Optimal conditions are determined by combining three pieces of information: the thermochemical equation (including delta H), the value of K (to understand the equilibrium position), and a graph of yield versus temperature or pressure.
items.why: VCE questions often provide a graph of yield versus pressure at different temperatures and ask students to explain the trend using the thermochemical equation. The ability to integrate multiple sources of information is a higher-order skill.
items.example: A graph showing ammonia yield increasing with pressure at all temperatures, and decreasing with temperature at all pressures, is consistent with the thermochemical equation N2 + 3H2 = 2NH3 (exothermic, fewer gas moles on product side). Lower temperature and higher pressure both favour higher yield.
